titleStmt.title: Scheduling and Shaping of Complex Task Activations for Mixed-Criticality Systems

analytic.title: Scheduling and Shaping of Complex Task Activations for Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper, we present a new schedulability test that can cope with complex activation patterns for mixed-criticality systems. Under this analysis we proceed to present a shaping approach that can adaptively make use of system slack to improve the quality of service to less critical tasks. Compared with the state-of-the-art scheduling analysis, our scheduling analysis is more effective in handling the case that activation events can be backlogged and task deadlines can be arbitrary; and the shaping approach furthermore reduces the dropped jobs of less critical tasks without jeopardizing the guarantee to critical tasks. Extensive simulations and real-life deployment in Raspberry Pi 3 board confirm the effectiveness of our proposed schedulability test and shaping approach.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Today's emerging embedded systems are performing more complex and diverse tasks on a single platform than ever before, as in this way costs and spaces can be reduced. Tasks in a system often have different criticalities and thus should be guaranteed to different degrees. This type of system is called mixed criticality system (Mcs). A typical example of Mcs is the unmanned aerial vehicle system that needs to guarantee the correctness more for tasks related to vehicle safety than for tasks only related to some vehicle missions. A common assumption of dual-criticality scheduling is to guarantee the schedulability of all tasks when no tasks overrun their less rigorous execution thresholds (normal mode) and the schedulability of only critical tasks when they overrun (critical mode). Since the less critical tasks are not required to be schedulable in critical mode, they are often supposed to be removed after entering the critical mode.

Motivation. In such certifiable mixed-criticality realtime systems, the task is often modeled as the sporadic activation pattern that only defines a minimum inter-activation interval (also called period) [3,4]. Although the results based on the analysis of sporadic tasks can provide some insights for classic activation patterns like periodic activations, those results are indeed pessimistic to accommodate the complex activation tasks. A simple example is illustrated in Fig. 1, where a task is activated every 4 time units, while there is a jitter of 1 time unit in every activation. In this case, the minimum distance between two task activations is 2. If this task is modeled as a sporadic task, the estimated number of task activations within 14 is 8. However, the fact is that at most 5 activations would happen within 14. Such task may be mixed-criticality schedulable, which however will be tested unschedulable under the sporadic task assumption.

In fact, complex task activations are nevertheless not uncommon in real-time systems [6,16,18]. In the automotive systems [18], tasks in a processing unit are often triggered by external events coming from other devices. The arrival patterns of most external event streams are neither periodic nor periodic with a jitter, but with some peculiarities that are difficult to be captured by the sporadic task model. In order to precisely analyze the effect of event arrival pattern on the system behavior, the framework of Real-Time Calculus [16] adopts a more general task activation model, arrival curve, to compute the task response time or maximum backlogged events. Stemming from the theory of network calculus [13], the arrival curve effectively expresses the maximum arrival events within any interval, which provides more accurate information on task activations than the sporadic model. In this paper, we adopt the arrival curve to model task activations, and present the schedulability analysis under the context of mixed-criticality system, i.e., tasks with different criticalities should be guaranteed to their own criticality levels. Furthermore, we propose a shaping approach to further improve the system performance by allowing less critical tasks to run in critical mode, while providing the same guarantee to critical tasks. Related Work. While both the mixed-criticality schedulability analysis and the slack scheduling approaches are not new (see a review [3]), they have their own limitations: the former provides the schedulability analysis to critical and less critical tasks while being limited in sporadic task model; the latter is either limited to the periodic task model or ignores the schedulability guarantee of less critical tasks by adopting the arrival curve model. The work of this paper is to extend the state-of-the-art mixed-criticality scheduling approach to analyze the schedulability of the arrival curve model under the earliest-deadline-first (EDF). We further proceed to propose a shaping approach to improve the system performance. However, this is not a trivial extension.

On the one hand, an important assumption of the existing schedulability analysis is that the task deadline should not be greater than its period. In this way there will be at most one backlogged event at the mode-switching moment. This assumption becomes unrealistic if we adopt the arrival curve model that admits burst events, as burst events are easy to be accumulated. Indeed, how to handle the task state at the time of mode-switch is significant in testing its schedulability. We should be neither pessimistic on their executions before the mode-switch as it has negative impact on the accumulated events, nor optimistic as it may lead 978-1-5090-0602-1/18/$31.00 ©2018 IEEE 1D-1 to the unreliability of the schedulability test. Nevertheless, it remains an open problem to test the system schedulability with mixed-criticality tasks whose activation events can be accumulated or deadlines can be arbitrary.

On the other hand, most previous shaping approaches [14,15,17] shape the arrival events to conform to the offline computed bound, where the offline computed bound is often too pessimistic for serving less critical tasks. In order to get rid of this scheduling pessimism, the online information should be used to calculate a tighter bound.

Contributions. In this paper, we propose to use the minimum distance function (Mdf) to represent the minimum distances of task activations modeled by arrival curves, based on which we introduce the effective deadlines to clarify that some jobs must have finished earlier than their absolute deadlines. The introduction of effective deadlines bypasses the problem of bounding the backlogged events at the modeswitching time and also helps to provide a tighter schedulability test. After the system enter into the critical mode, we propose a shaping approach to further run less critical tasks. To be specific, we use the task procrastination techniques [11] to detect the run-time slack that can be safely used to run less critical tasks without reducing the guarantee to critical tasks. The less critical jobs will be dropped only when their executions hamper the schedulability of critical tasks. Simulation results and real-life deployments confirm that the proposed approaches are more effective in improving system performance in terms of schedulability, service guarantee to less critical tasks. The implementation also demonstrates that the shaping approach is lightweight regarding to the computation overhead.

div.head: Event Model
div.p: We consider that a task is activated by an activating event [6,16], and task activations are expressed by an event stream. To denote the upper bound of arrival events within any interval of a length Δ, we introduce arrival curve [13].
Definition 1 (Arrival Curve). The arrival curve αi(Δ) returns an upper bound on the number of events of a task τi that may occur in any time interval of a length Δ.

The arrival curve only provides an upper bound on the number of events. In order to know specific minimal distances among any events, we rely on a concept similar to the arrival curve: minimum distance function [6].

Definition 2 (Minimum Distance Function). The minimum distance function δ(q) is a pseudo super-additive 1 function, which returns a lower bound on the time interval between the first and the last event of any sequence of q + 1 event occurrences.

The minimum distance function is an inverse description of upper arrival curve. For example, δ(k) = Δ k denotes that, the first and the last event of any sequence of k + 1 events is at least Δ k time units apart, i.e., α(δ(k)) = k + 1.

The concept of arrival curve or minimum distance function substationally generalizes conventional event stream models, such as sporadic, periodic, periodic with jitter, and arbitrary event streams. For instance, for the arbitrary events modeled with the period p, the jitter j, and the minimum inter 1 For pseudo super-additive we denote the property of a function δ that ∀a, b ∈ N + : δ(a+b) ≥ δ(a)+δ(b). It corresponds to the property of "good" arrival functions in [13].
arrival distance d between successive two events, its upper arrival curve is

div.p: This arrival pattern is called pjd pattern that is often used as a typical example of the complex arrival pattern in many previous works [9,11,12].

div.head: Mixed-Criticality System Settings
div.p: This paper assumes a dual-criticality task set τ = {τ1, ..., τn} is given to be scheduled. Each task τi is defined by its arrival curve or minimum distance function, relative deadline, Wcet and criticality: (αi or δi(q), Di, C i , Li), where C i = (Ci(LO), Ci(HI)) that represents a task two level Wcets and Li represents a task criticality. We call the dualcriticality levels as the LO criticality and the HI criticality. The Wcets of LO-critical tasks are modeled on the LO criticality, and the Wcets of HI-critical tasks are modeled on both criticality. That is, each LO-critical task only has a LO Wcet, and each HI-critical task has a LO Wcet and a HI Wcet. For HI-critical tasks, the Wcets on the HI criticality are non-decreasing when compared to their Wcets on the LO criticality, i.e., ∀τi ∈ τ H : Ci(LO) ≤ Ci(HI) where τ H and τ L denote the set of HI-critical and LO-critical tasks, respectively. Besides, in this paper the denotation x 0 is the abbreviation of max(0, x).

The system is scheduled as the adaptive run-time scheduling algorithm [2]. That is, the system starts in LO mode (normal mode), where all tasks are assumed not to exceed their LO Wcets. If any HI-critical task exceeds its LO Wcet, the system transits immediately to the HI mode (critical mode), where only HI-critical tasks are required to be schedulable. For every task, there is only one relative deadline Di. But in order to apply the earlist-deadline-first schedule on it, its relative deadline in LO mode can be artificially decreased [1]. Hence, Di(LO) ≤ Di(HI) = Di, where Di(LO) and Di(HI) are the relative deadlines of a task in LO and HI modes, respectively.

div.head: Schedulable Conditions
div.p: In the schedulability test of a task set, we rely on the demand-bound function (Dbf) [4] that upper-bounds the maximum demand of them over any interval.

div.head: Definition 3 (Demand-bound function). The demandbound function dbf(τi, Δ) gives an upper bound on the maximum possible execution demand of the task τi in any time interval of length Δ, where demand is calculated as the total amount of required execution time of events with their whole scheduling windows within the time interval.
div.p: For a non-mixed-criticality system with a task set τ , the following inequality guarantees the schedulability of this task set:
div.formula: τ i ∈τ dbf(τ i , Δ) ≤ Δ, ∀Δ ≥ 0,
div.p: where Δ represents the supply of a dedicated unit-speed uniprocessor. Analogously, in Mcss, the task set is schedulable if the Dbfs in LO and HI modes are smaller than the provided supply of this platform [4], i.e., Condition 1 : ∀Δ ≥ 0 : Therefore, to determine the schedulability of a task set, one only needs to derive the Dbfs in both modes.
div.formula: τ i ∈τ dbf LO (τ i , Δ) ≤ Δ, Condition 2 : ∀Δ ≥ 0 : τ i ∈HI(τ ) dbf HI (τ i , Δ) ≤ Δ.

div.head: Demand-Bound Function in LO mode
div.p: If the system is in LO mode, every task behaves as a normal task with parameters (αi(Δ) or δi(q), Ci(LO), Di(LO)). According to the framework of real-time calculus [16], a tight demand bound function (Dbf) of a task τi is that
div.formula: dbf LO (τ i , Δ) = α i (Δ -D i (LO)) • C i (LO).

div.head: Demand-Bound Function in HI mode
div.p: The derivation of Dbf in HI mode needs to know the maximum required execution times within any time interval in HI mode to guarantee that events within this interval can meet their deadlines, where events of an interval may include the carry-over jobs (released but not finished at the mode-switching time). In order to know dbfHI(τi, Δ), we need to upper-bound the maximum number of deadlines of τi within any interval of a length Δ in HI mode. To do so, the as-early-as-possible event arrivals are assumed because this assumption is able to accumulate the most number of deadlines in the shortest time. Hence, when given a time length Δ in HI mode, the maximum number of deadlines is αi(Δ) and the demand is αi(Δ) • Ci(HI). However, this demand ignores that events may have been finished earlier than their deadlines if those events need to keep schedulable. To explore those finished executions, we introduce the effective deadlines to define the timing constraints that are able to guarantee the system schedulable in LO mode.

div.head: Effective Deadlines
div.p: The timing constraints require that the finishing time of any event must not exceed its absolute deadline, where the absolute deadline of an event is the time point that is the sum of its arrival time and its relative deadline.

For some event streams, their events may be required to be finished earlier than their absolute deadlines so that there will be enough slacks for processing following events. The effective deadline is thus defined to show this timing constraint.

div.head: Definition 4 (Effective Deadline). The effective deadline of an event is referred to its allowable largest finish time that guarantees other events of this task meet their absolute deadlines.
div.p: We use AD(e) and ED(e) to respectively denote the absolute deadline and the effective deadline of an event e. Example 1. An example is used to explain the differences between effective deadlines and absolute deadline. For a task τi activated by a pjd event stream with p = 10, j = 30, d = 2, the as-early-as-possible arrival events are shown in Fig. 2. div.head: A SHAPING APPROACH
div.p: After the system enters into HI mode, only HI-critical tasks need to be guaranteed. Thus, a lot of existing scheduling approaches abandon LO-critical tasks in HI mode in order to sufficiently guarantee HI-critical tasks. However, abandoning all LO-critical tasks may not be necessary as the system may have some "free" slacks that can used to run LO-critical tasks. Such slacks exist due to the system not fully loaded or HI-critical tasks finishing earlier than our given thresholds. In this section, we present a shaping approach to exploit such slacks to let LO-critical tasks run in HI mode.

The shaping approach is inspired by the task procrastination technique in hard real-time system [11], where task executions are deliberately delayed by forcing the processor in sleep state without missing any deadlines. Analogously, the processing of LO-critical tasks is considered as the resources procrastination on HI-critical tasks in the sense that their executions obstruct the executions on HI-critical tasks. If the processing time of LO-critical tasks is less than the feasible procrastination interval, the timeliness of HI-critical tasks can be guaranteed. Therefore, we detect the feasible procrastination interval online and schedule LO-critical jobs only if their executions will not violate the feasible procrastination interval. Similar approaches can be seen in [7][8][9][10].

div.head: Shaping Workflow
div.p: With the shaping approach, LO-critical tasks are not prevented from executing in HI mode, but are constrained within a certain execution extent. To specify such extent, a term named LO-critical Budget (LO-B) is introduced. LO-B at some time t is a safe upper bound on the total amount of time that the processor can work on LO-critical tasks after time t. In other words, all HI-critical tasks can meet their deadlines after time t if the processor does not execute LO-critical tasks for more than LO-B time units.

Based on LO-B, the system in HI mode will schedule HIand LO-critical tasks as Fig. 5. First of all, we set up a LO-B timer. Based on the principle of earliest-deadlinefirst schedule, the task with the earliest deadline will be executed prior to other tasks. If this task is HI-critical, the system allows it to run without the constraint of LO-B. If it is LO-critical, its execution will be constrained by LO-B. In a case that this task does not finish till the LO-B timer times out (time instant t ), the system will update LO-B. The new updated LO-B will either allow this task to run further if the new LO-B is greater than zero, or drop it otherwise. Compared to the previous shaping approaches, the key advantage of our shaping approach is able to detect and use the runtime processing slack as much as possible by updating LO-B whenever it runs up.

div.head: Updating LO-B
div.p: When LO-B timer times out with the running of LOcritical tasks, it may be possible to further allow LO-critical tasks to run because the actual arrival events of HI-critical tasks are less than the worst-case assumption or because they finish earlier than given budgets. We need to know the task demand bound of HI-critical tasks so that the updated LO-B will not violate the schedulability of HI-critical tasks. To model the task demand at runtime, we rely on the task demand bound function (Dbf) online and denote it as dbfHI(τi, Δ, t), where dbfHI(τi, Δ, t) represents the maximum required execution time of events of τi in HI mode over any interval of length Δ after time t. div.head: EVALUATIONS
div.p: We now evaluate the performance of our proposed approaches with state-of-the-art scheduling techniques by extensive simulations and implementations in Raspberry Pi 3 board.

div.head: Random Task Set Generation
div.p: We generate the task set in the same way as [4]. In particular, a random task set is generated as a pjd activation task (see Eq. 1) by starting with an empty task set τ = ∅, where random tasks are successively added.

The random task set is generated as follows: The task set utilization is a value of (x + 0.5)/30, where x ∈ {0, 1, ..., 29}; The probability of a random task being HI-critical is 0.5; Ci(LO) is drawn from the uniform distribution over {1, 2, ..., 10}; Ci(HI) is drawn from the uniform distribution over {Ci(LO), Ci(LO) + 1, ..., 4 • Ci(LO)} if Li = HI; The period pi is drawn from the uniform distribution over {Ci(Li), Ci(Li) +1, ..., 200}; The jitter ji is set as X •pi; The minimum inter distance di is set as Y •pi; The relative deadline is set as that Di(LO) = Di(HI) = pi.

div.head: Baseline Schedulability Test
div.p: To evaluate the schedulability and shaping performance of our proposed approaches, we introduce three existing schedulability tests as baselines. In order to distinguish the proposed approach with them, the schedulability test proposed in this paper is called arrival curve based schedulability test (abbreviated as AC-Sched).

Since the existing scheduling analysis can only analyze the schedulability of sporadic tasks, we need to transform the pjd task to the sporadic task so that their schedulability can be determined by the existing scheduling analysis. According to the definition of sporadic task model, a safe transformation is to use the minimum distance of any two events of a pjd task, i.e., σ(1) of its minimum distance function, as the period of its corresponding sporadic task. Then, three stateof-the-art schedulability testing approaches, Greedy,AMCmax,EDF-VD, respectively pro-posed in [1,2,4], are used as baselines to evaluate our proposed approaches.

div.head: Schedulability Results
div.p: In our experiments, for each target utilization, 1000 task sets are generated, from which the ratio that task sets pass the schedulability test is used to represent the effectiveness of a schedulability test.

We investigate four parameter sets: (X , Y) = {(0, 0), (0.5, 0), (3, 0.2), (3, 0.6)}. If (X , Y) = (0, 0), all tasks are sporadic tasks. Fig. 6(a) shows that AC-sched has the same performance as Greedy on scheduling sporadic tasks. However, in the three other parameter sets, the event arrival pattern either has a jitter or a burst. Fig. 6(b), 6(b), 6(d) confirm that our approach outperforms the existing three approaches to a large extent on the three other cases. Greedy is shown to be the effective among the three existing approaches.

div.head: Shaping Results
div.p: We implement the three existing scheduling approaches on top of a linux user-space framework SF3P [5]. Furthermore, we implement the proposed shaping approach based on the AC-Sched test. This shaping approach is abbreviated as AC-Shaping for easiness. All implementations are tested on a host of Raspberry Pi 3 board with a 1.2GHz ARMv8 CPU.

We investigate the parameter X varying from 0.2 to 1 by fixing Y = 0; and investigate the parameter Y varying from 0.6 to 1 by fixing X = 3. For each parameter set, 50 task sets, each with a utilization of 0. and tested scheduable by all above schedulability tests. The probability of a HI-critical task exceeding its LO Wcet is 0.005. This probability is set deliberately high because we want to get the distinguished results in a reasonable running time. Every task set is run for 15 minutes. The average number of dropped jobs in each task set is shown in Fig. 7, where the AC-Shaping reduces the dropped jobs to less than one fourth of the other scheduling approaches.

The shaping approach is based on updating LO-B, whose computation expense was also investigated. We measure 200 updating expenses for each task set. As shown on a logarithmic scale in Fig. 8, with the increase of task set size, the computation expense increases. But even for a task set with 30 tasks, the average computation expense is only a little more than 1ms. This result confirms that the shaping overhead is actually small.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we have presented a new approach to analyze the schedulability of arbitrarily activated tasks. Compared with the existing approaches that often model task activations as sporadic pattern, our approach is more effective by using the arrival curve to model the arbitrary activation pattern. As a result, the proposed schedulability test in mixed-criticality systems becomes more applicable as it can handle the case that activation events can be backlogged and task deadlines can be arbitrary. Furthermore, we have proposed a shaping approach that is able to keep LOcritical jobs in critical mode by exploring and making use of the run-time processing slack. The extensive simulations and implementations on an embedded platform confirm the advantages of our proposed schedulability test and shaping approach.
